'''Toniann Pitassi'''  is a Canadian-American mathematician and [[computer scientist]] specializing in [[computational complexity theory]]. She is currently Jeffrey L. and Brenda Bleustein Professor of Engineering at [[Columbia University]] and was Bell Research Chair at the [[University of Toronto]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=toniann pitassi {{!}} Department of Computer Science, Columbia University |url=https://www.cs.columbia.edu/tag/toniann-pitassi/ |access-date=May 4, 2022 |website=www.cs.columbia.edu}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Four Columbians Elected to the National Academy of Sciences |url=https://news.columbia.edu/news/four-columbians-elected-national-academy-sciences |access-date=May 4, 2022 |website=Columbia News |language=en}}</ref>

==Academic career==
A native of [[Pittsburgh]], Pitassi earned bachelor's and master's degrees at [[Pennsylvania State University]] before moving to the [[University of Toronto]] for her doctoral studies; she earned her PhD in 1992 from Toronto under the supervision of [[Stephen Cook]]. After postdoctoral studies at the [[University of California, San Diego]] and faculty positions at the [[University of Pittsburgh]] and [[University of Arizona]], she returned to Toronto in 2001, and was a professor in the [[Department of Computer Science (University of Toronto)|Department of Computer Science]] and [[Department of Mathematics (University of Toronto)|Department of Mathematics]] at the University of Toronto until 2021, when she joined the faculty of [[Columbia University]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~toni/|title=Toniann Pitassi|website=University of Toronto|access-date=December 31, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{MathGenealogy |id=80101}}</ref>

She was an invited speaker at [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Berlin in 1998.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mathunion.org/icm-plenary-and-invited-speakers?combine=Pitassi|title=ICM Plenary and Invited Speakers|website=International Mathematical Union|language=en|access-date=December 31, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Pitassi, Toniann|chapter=Unsolvable systems of equations and proof complexity|title=Doc. Math. (Bielefeld) Extra Vol. ICM Berlin, 1998, vol. III|year=1998|pages=451–458|chapter-url=https://www.elibm.org/ft/10011601000}}</ref> She was the program chair for the 2012 [[Symposium on Theory of Computing]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cs.nyu.edu/~stoc2012/default.htm|title=STOC 2012 - 44th ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing|website=[[New York University]], Computer Science Department|access-date=December 31, 2017}}</ref> From September through December 2017, she was a visiting professor at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/toniann-pitassi|title=Toniann Pitassi|work=Institute for Advanced Study|access-date=December 31, 2017|language=en}}</ref>

==Research==
Pitassi's research has largely focused on [[proof complexity]], a branch of [[computational complexity theory]] that seeks [[upper and lower bounds]] on the lengths of [[mathematical proof]]s of [[Proposition|logical propositions]] within various formalized proof systems. The goal of this study is to use these bounds to understand both the [[time complexity]] of proof-finding procedures, and the relative strengths of different proof systems.

Research contributions that she has made in this area include exponential lower bounds for [[Frege system|Frege proofs]] of the [[pigeonhole principle]],<ref>{{harvtxt|Pitassi|Beame|Impagliazzo|1993}}.</ref> exponential lower bounds for the [[cutting-plane method]] applied to propositions derived from the [[maximum clique problem]],<ref>{{harvtxt|Bonet|Pitassi|Raz|1997}}.</ref> exponential lower bounds for [[Resolution (logic)|resolution]] proofs of dense random [[3-satisfiability]] instances,<ref>{{harvtxt|Beame|Pitassi|1996}}; {{harvtxt|Beame|Karp|Pitassi|Saks|2002}}.</ref> and subexponential upper bounds for the same dense random instances using the [[Davis–Putnam algorithm]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Beame|Karp|Pitassi|Saks|1998}}; {{harvtxt|Beame|Karp|Pitassi|Saks|2002}}.</ref> With various coauthors, she has several expositions and surveys: on proof complexity in general,<ref>{{citation | last1 = Beame | first1 = Paul | last2 = Pitassi | first2 = Toniann | title = Propositional Proof Complexity: Past, Present and Future | journal = Bulletin EATCS | year = 1998 | issue=65 | pages = 66–89 | url = https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/eccc-reports/1998/TR98-067/index.html}}</ref> on algebraic proof complexity,<ref>{{citation | last1 = Pitassi | first1 = Toniann | last2 = Tzameret | first2 = Iddo | title = Algebraic proof complexity: progress, frontiers and challenges | journal = ACM SIGLOG News | volume = 3 | issue = 3 | year = 2016 | doi = 10.1145/2984450.2984455 | pages = 21–43}}</ref> and on semialgebraic proof complexity.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Fleming | first1 = Noah | last2 = Kothari | first2= Pravesh | last3 = Pitassi | first3 = Toniann | title = Semialgebraic Proofs and Efficient Algorithm Design | journal = Foundations and Trends in Theoretical Computer Science | publisher = now Publishers | volume = 14 | issue = 1–2 | year = 2019 | pages = 1–221 | doi = 10.1561/0400000086 | url = https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2019/106/| doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Recognition==
Pitassi was elected as an [[ACM Fellow]] in 2018 for "contributions to research and education in the fields of computational and proof complexity".<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.acm.org/media-center/2018/december/fellows-2018|title=2018 ACM Fellows Honored for Pivotal Achievements that Underpin the Digital Age|publisher=[[Association for Computing Machinery]]|date=December 5, 2018}}</ref>

Pitassi was also the recipient of the [[EATCS]] (European Association for Theoretical Computer Science) Award in 2021 for her "fundamental and wide-ranging contributions to computational complexity".<ref>{{citation|url=https://eatcs.org/index.php/component/content/article/1-news/2877-the-eatcs-award-2021-laudatio-for-toniann-toni-pitassi-|title=The EATCS Award 2021 - Laudatio for Toniann (Toni) Pitassi|publisher=European Association for Theoretical Computer Science|date=June 4, 2021}}</ref>

She was named to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2022.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=2022 NAS Election |url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2022-nas-election.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220503174757/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2022-nas-election.html |archive-date=May 3, 2022 |access-date=May 4, 2022 |website=nasonline.org}}</ref>
